claims.text: The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.

A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.

Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.
Orb-v3 models achieve competitive thermal conductivity prediction (κSRME), demonstrating direct models can yield smooth second- and third-order derivatives of the potential energy surface.
The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%.

AFLOW: an automatic framework for high-throughput materials discovery AFLOW high-throughput materials discovery framework AFLOW can automatically calculate a wide suite of physical observables across a large database of structures with minimal human intervention. AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management. AFLOW provides a standardized definition of Brillouin‑zone integration paths for all 14 Bravais lattices, filling a gap in the literature. AFLOW reproduces experimental phonon dispersion curves for face‑centered cubic Rhodium, showing excellent agreement with measured data. AFLOW’s cage‑finding algorithm identifies interstitial sites via a topological method, finding 14 cages (6 octahedral, 8 tetrahedral) that reduce to 5 symmetrically inequivalent positions, with radii of 2.2225 Å (octahedral) and 1.9248 Å (tetrahedral). AFLOW can automatically generate high‑index surface slabs for complex multicomponent compounds, demonstrated for (001), (110) and (111) slabs of an fcc L10 binary.

S. Dasa K. Garikipati Using the IDNN reduces the computational cost of generating free‑energy data for continuum models by approximately two orders of magnitude compared with direct DFT sampling. Phase‑field simulations using the IDNN‑derived free‑energy density predict nucleation rates of the ordered phase at 260 K that are an order of magnitude higher than at 300 K, consistent with a larger free‑energy decrease (1 meV vs 0.5 meV per unit cell). Phase‑field simulations reproduce the lever‑rule mass fractions of ordered and disordered phases predicted by the Monte Carlo phase diagram after accounting for a slight shift in the order‑disorder boundaries from the IDNN free‑energy surface. Symmetry‑invariant polynomial features up to sixth order, constructed via the Reynolds operator, are used as inputs to the IDNN to respect the 384‑element symmetry group of the zig‑zag ordering. The IDNN framework is generalizable and can be applied to other intercalation compounds without modification of the network architecture.

MLIPs require substantial training data to learn the physics of the system, though this is becoming easier to meet as ab initio data becomes more plentiful and standardized. MLIPs are straightforward to iteratively improve by adding more training data, whereas improving PBPs often requires fundamental changes to underlying functional forms. Most MLIPs are trained on limited domains (1-10 elements) and cannot extrapolate to new elements or local structures not in training data. U-MLIPs generally have low energy and force errors compared to their ab initio training data. U-MLIPs systematically underpredict energies and forces due to softening of the potential energy surface, attributed to biased sampling in training datasets from DFT ionic relaxations near local PES minima. Each cataloged DFT structure provides one energy and 3N forces (N = number of atoms) for training universal MLIPs. DFT database size used to train U-MLIPs has increased by more than an order of magnitude each year, from roughly 2×10^5 in 2022 to 1.18×10^8 in 2024. Surface energy prediction errors are much more significant than bulk energy errors because surface structures were not present in U-MLIP training data.

Virtual Node Graph Neural Network for Full Phonon Prediction Three virtual node approaches were developed: vector virtual nodes (VVN) outputting 3m Γ-phonon branches, matrix virtual nodes (MVN) with m² 3×3 matrices, and momentum-dependent matrix virtual nodes (k-MVN) for full band structure prediction. Virtual Node Graph Neural Network (VGNN) enables graph neural networks to handle variable output dimensions by incorporating virtual nodes that resemble phonon dynamical matrices. VGNN achieves direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full phonon dispersion using only atomic coordinates as input without prior knowledge of interatomic forces. MVN outperforms VVN for Γ-phonon prediction, especially for complex materials, at the cost of slightly higher computational expense. The k-MVN model can handle phonon prediction for alloys ranging from binary to five-component high entropy alloys by encoding atomic composition through weighted atomic masses. For very complicated materials, VVN-predicted phonons tend to have higher frequencies than ground truth, and prediction loss becomes larger as input materials become more complicated. The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals. The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%. Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene. Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations. The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa). The GNN’s stress predictions are substantially more accurate than on‑the‑fly stress calculations from the force field, which exhibit higher errors. The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples. The GNN respects physical constraints, accurately capturing derivative properties such as stress fields that obey underlying physical laws, and predicts global properties (Young’s modulus, total potential energy) that follow known physical relationships and match MD results across different crystalline systems.

Machine learning a general purpose interatomic potential for silicon The Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) for silicon reproduces density functional theory reference results across a wide range of observable properties, including bulk crystal, liquid, amorphous phases, and point, line, and plane defects. For bulk elastic constants (B, C11, C12, C44) the GAP model achieves fractional errors of less than 10% relative to DFT, outperforming all other evaluated interatomic potentials. Surface energies of the (111), (110) and (100) silicon cleavage planes are predicted by GAP with errors of around 2% relative to DFT, which is comparable or better than other potentials. Combining a simple repulsive pair potential with a many‑body SOAP‑kernel term in the GAP framework yields meV‑per‑atom accuracy for silicon energetics. Using the GAP model enables simulations that would be prohibitively expensive with DFT, such as finite‑temperature phase‑boundary calculations, liquid self‑diffusivity, amorphous silicon formation by slow quench, and dynamic brittle fracture. A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations. Benchmark comparisons show that the new GAP model yields lower errors than previous GAP models for silicon.

The AFLOW Standard for High-Throughput Materials Science Calculations The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria. AFLOW calculations follow a standardized sequential workflow: RELAX1 → RELAX2 → STATIC → BANDS for materials in the Elements, ICSD, and Heusler databases. AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management. AFLOW’s cage‑finding algorithm identifies interstitial sites via a topological method, finding 14 cages (6 octahedral, 8 tetrahedral) that reduce to 5 symmetrically inequivalent positions, with radii of 2.2225 Å (octahedral) and 1.9248 Å (tetrahedral). AFLOW can automatically construct convex hulls for binary alloy systems at zero temperature using formation enthalpies from DFT calculations. MLIPs require substantial training data to learn the physics of the system, though this is becoming easier to meet as ab initio data becomes more plentiful and standardized. MLIPs are straightforward to iteratively improve by adding more training data, whereas improving PBPs often requires fundamental changes to underlying functional forms. Most MLIPs are trained on limited domains (1-10 elements) and cannot extrapolate to new elements or local structures not in training data. U-MLIPs generally have low energy and force errors compared to their ab initio training data. U-MLIPs systematically underpredict energies and forces due to softening of the potential energy surface, attributed to biased sampling in training datasets from DFT ionic relaxations near local PES minima. Each cataloged DFT structure provides one energy and 3N forces (N = number of atoms) for training universal MLIPs. DFT database size used to train U-MLIPs has increased by more than an order of magnitude each year, from roughly 2×10^5 in 2022 to 1.18×10^8 in 2024. Surface energy prediction errors are much more significant than bulk energy errors because surface structures were not present in U-MLIP training data.

Machine-learning based interatomic potential for amorphous carbon GAP radial and angular distribution functions for liquid and amorphous carbon closely match DFT reference results, including peak locations, extents, and overall curve shapes. GAP recovers three- and four-membered rings that are key features of liquid and low-density amorphous carbon structures, which empirical potentials (Tersoff/Brenner) fail to predict. GAP predictions for Young's modulus of amorphous carbon agree very well with experimental values at all relevant densities, while screened Tersoff potential captures the trend but significantly overestimates absolute values. GAP sp3 concentration predictions are closer to DFT reference than empirical Brenner and Tersoff potentials, particularly at lower densities; empirical potentials underestimate sp3 concentration in tetrahedral amorphous carbon. For amorphous carbon with 3.7 Å cutoff radius, the lowest achievable standard deviation of force components is approximately 1 eV/Å due to fundamental nonlocality limits, representing a maximum accuracy bound for any finite-range interatomic potential. DFT-based methods are practically limited to systems of a few hundred atoms, making generation of 8,000-atom amorphous carbon structures impossible with DFT-MD even on state-of-the-art supercomputers. amorphous carbon structures

For bulk elastic constants (B, C11, C12, C44) the GAP model achieves fractional errors of less than 10% relative to DFT, outperforming all other evaluated interatomic potentials. Surface energies of the (111), (110) and (100) silicon cleavage planes are predicted by GAP with errors of around 2% relative to DFT, which is comparable or better than other potentials. Combining a simple repulsive pair potential with a many‑body SOAP‑kernel term in the GAP framework yields meV‑per‑atom accuracy for silicon energetics. Using the GAP model enables simulations that would be prohibitively expensive with DFT, such as finite‑temperature phase‑boundary calculations, liquid self‑diffusivity, amorphous silicon formation by slow quench, and dynamic brittle fracture. A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations. Benchmark comparisons show that the new GAP model yields lower errors than previous GAP models for silicon.

MLIPs require substantial training data to learn the physics of the system, though this is becoming easier to meet as ab initio data becomes more plentiful and standardized. MLIPs are straightforward to iteratively improve by adding more training data, whereas improving PBPs often requires fundamental changes to underlying functional forms. Most MLIPs are trained on limited domains (1-10 elements) and cannot extrapolate to new elements or local structures not in training data. U-MLIPs generally have low energy and force errors compared to their ab initio training data. U-MLIPs systematically underpredict energies and forces due to softening of the potential energy surface, attributed to biased sampling in training datasets from DFT ionic relaxations near local PES minima. Each cataloged DFT structure provides one energy and 3N forces (N = number of atoms) for training universal MLIPs. DFT database size used to train U-MLIPs has increased by more than an order of magnitude each year, from roughly 2×10^5 in 2022 to 1.18×10^8 in 2024. Surface energy prediction errors are much more significant than bulk energy errors because surface structures were not present in U-MLIP training data.

machine learning potential training Simulating diffusion properties of solid-state electrolytes via a neural network potential: Performance and training scheme For NASICON, training starting from PFF-MD configurations with 480 atoms achieves convergence during the first training loop with activation energy around 0.2 eV. For NASICON, training starting from FPMD configurations with 80 atoms fails to converge even after three training loops with activation energies spanning 0.2-0.4 eV. Starting the training loop with PFF-MD configurations leads to faster convergence than starting with short FPMD trajectories because larger simulation cells can be used. Training set cleaning procedures including minimum ion-ion distance cutoff, energy/force outlier removal, and loss condition monitoring are necessary to help the algorithm converge to a physical model. The proposed training protocol based on augmenting the training set via intermediate molecular dynamics simulations can assess the quality of approximate trajectories and computed physical properties. Starting the training loop with sufficient data sampling a relevant portion of phase space is important for obtaining generalizable models.

surface energy prediction for amorphous materials The Materials Project aims to reduce the typical 10–20 year timeline for advanced material development by providing large‑scale accurate information, thereby accelerating discovery for clean energy, electronics, and other sectors. SchNet provides rotationally invariant energy predictions and rotationally equivariant, energy‑conserving force predictions by defining forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy. On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training. Continuous-filter convolutions produce smoother energy predictions than discrete filters, as illustrated in Figure 1. On the QM9 benchmark, SchNet attains a mean absolute error of 0.31 kcal/mol for total‑energy prediction with 110 k training examples, outperforming DTNN (0.84) and enn‑s2s (0.45). Fine‑tuning an energy model on a benzene vibrational spectrum improves spectrum predictions for unseen molecules such as toluene and phenol. Training universal interatomic potential models with forces, stresses, and magnetic moments substantially improves stability‑prediction performance compared with energy‑only models, enhancing both classification metrics (F1, DAF) and regression metrics (MAE, RMSE).

AFLOW calculations follow a standardized sequential workflow: RELAX1 → RELAX2 → STATIC → BANDS for materials in the Elements, ICSD, and Heusler databases. Default NKPPRA values for non-BANDS calculations vary by database: Binary Alloy uses 6000 for RELAX, Heusler uses 10000 for STATIC and 6000 for RELAX, and ICSD uses 10000 for STATIC and 8000 for RELAX. The AFLOWLIB repository contains calculated properties of over 625,000 materials across Binary Alloy Project, Electronic Structure database, Heusler database, and Elements database. DFT+U corrections are applied to the entire ICSD database and certain Heusler database entries containing O, S, Se, and F elements, but not to the Binary Alloy database. Specific Ueff parameters are defined for d-block elements (Table 4) and U, J parameters for f-block elements (Table 5) to correct self-interaction error in DFT+U calculations, with values ranging from 1.9 eV (In) to 7.5 eV (Zn). Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV. BANDS calculations use 128 k-points per segment for single element structures and 20 k-points for compounds along high-symmetry paths. STATIC

Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations. The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals. The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%. The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa). Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene. The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples. The Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA) GNN model achieves the lowest mean and variance of test mean‑squared error among GCN, GAT, and MPNN (sum and max) variants on the polycrystalline graphene dataset. Design of de novo atomic structures using GNNs combined with genetic algorithms

Each cataloged DFT structure provides one energy and 3N forces (N = number of atoms) for training universal MLIPs. MLIPs require substantial training data to learn the physics of the system, though this is becoming easier to meet as ab initio data becomes more plentiful and standardized. MLIPs are straightforward to iteratively improve by adding more training data, whereas improving PBPs often requires fundamental changes to underlying functional forms. Most MLIPs are trained on limited domains (1-10 elements) and cannot extrapolate to new elements or local structures not in training data. U-MLIPs generally have low energy and force errors compared to their ab initio training data. Training U-MLIPs on energies, forces, and stresses yields the most physically accurate potential, with stresses required for modeling structural phase transformations or NPT ensemble molecular dynamics. U-MLIPs systematically underpredict energies and forces due to softening of the potential energy surface, attributed to biased sampling in training datasets from DFT ionic relaxations near local PES minima. For LLZO, results are quite insensitive to the choice of cell volume (NPT equilibrated vs experimental cif-file values) for producing the initial training set.

definitions.candidate_pool: All snapshot nodes, including unusual types; soft priors never filter. R0 is all-type surface-only to isolate the R1 context increment; legacy routed type-prefixed flat remains separately archived.
definitions.cost: Each actually computed query/text-vector dot product costs one; identical stored text vectors are computed once per query view and reused across fields/entities. Offline encoding/index construction excluded and timed.
definitions.grouping: Exact normalized names only, no fuzzy merges. Same resolved target denominator in every stage; report number of underlying nodes covered by top-K groups.
definitions.missing_fields: Contribute zero with fixed weights, without renormalizing available fields; this favors entities with documented context and is a design limitation.
definitions.evidence: Context shared through a presenting article is a separate lower-weight claim_article field; ordinary cited-work provenance is not evidence that every article claim concerns that work.
definitions.resolution: Canonical exact/alias coverage distinct from representable evidence/composites. Composite representability requires all canonical components plus shared article provenance; this is not proof of functional composition.
definitions.metrics: Primary entity recall uses canonical exact/alias targets only. Representable recall separately includes evidence and fully graph-supported composites (all components required). Raw lower bound retains all expected targets. Precision gives one credit per recovered canonical target at fixed K; duplicate mentions cannot add credit. MRR is reciprocal first relevant rank over the exhaustive ranking.
definitions.source: Source hit/recall measures provenance overlap, never semantic entailment. Required sources outside the snapshot remain in resolution coverage and raw lower-bound denominators.
definitions.hierarchy_gate: Implement contextual hierarchy only after the flat original-question checkpoint demonstrates nontrivial recovery; original hierarchy construction remains unchanged.

contextual_retrieval.hierarchy_status: not_implemented: apply flat-quality decision gate before adding contextual hierarchy

protocol.formulation: Our query-semantic restart adaptation; Zhou section 7 uses initial labels, not query retrieval. f=(1-alpha)*(I-alpha*Theta)^-1*y.
protocol.defaults: alpha=.85, M=100, tolerance=1e-8, max_iterations=100, RRF k=60 with average ranks for exact score ties; sensitivities do not select defaults
protocol.answer_pool: Fixed configured scientific entity types; all node types remain propagation intermediates. H0 has no post-hoc soft prior; H1/H2/H3 inherit R3 soft prior only via RRF.
protocol.comparison: Historical R0/R1/R3 are recomputed unchanged, plus R3_answer_pool control and atomic answer-only control to separate filtering from propagation.
protocol.weights: Native exports without explicit weight use 1; H0 uniform relation multipliers. H3 semantic priors fixed before outcomes; vertex degrees recomputed with weighted W.
protocol.costs: Seed dot products and sparse applications separate. H1/H2/H3 standalone cost sums measured components; actual incremental cache reuse also logged. Diagnostics/paths and model encoding excluded from search time.
protocol.sensitivity: One-at-a-time alpha with M100, and M50/200 with alpha.85, on H0 and H3. No retrospective optimum selected.
protocol.type_b: Existing source/evidence pipeline and all historical Type B outputs unchanged; diffusion run contains Type A only.
protocol.null: One arity/relation/weight-preserving membership shuffle with seed42; degrees, connectivity and type mixes are not preserved.
protocol.pairwise: Existing weight-conserving clique projection; same Zhou arity2 operator = half(identity + symmetric normalized adjacency) on nonisolates; not ordinary non-lazy PPR. Native Theta itself is linear and has an equivalent weighted pair expansion, so success is not proof of irreducible higher-order expressivity.
